articles.text: Another revolution is in progress in Mexico, Manuel Rodriguez is the leader.
articles.summary: Brief note that a revolution led by Manuel Rodriguez is in progress in Mexico.

articles.text: Jay Gould has decided to entirely abandon all stock speculation and except for his interests as an investor in many concerns, will turn over his whole business to his son.
articles.summary: Jay Gould to quit stock speculation and turn his business over to his son.

articles.text: A man named Hopkins has invented a telephone on an entirely new principle by which the sound of the voice can be transmitted as far as a telegram can be sent. It bids fair to run the Bell and other telephones out of the market.
articles.summary: A man named Hopkins has invented a long-distance telephone said to threaten the Bell telephone.

articles.text: Chicago reminds one constantly of Griffin's Irishman who "wanted the earth and some of the outside." She is now making preparations to hold a World's Fair there in 1892, the anniversary of the discovery of America, and will probably succeed in her endeavor.
articles.summary: Chicago preparing to hold a World's Fair in 1892.

articles.text: Ada Sweet, the Chicago pension agent who created such a flutter some time since by refusing to resign and wrote a severe letter signing herself "Ada Sweet, Spinster," was married recently to a man named Carter. Remarks from Puck, to the effect that it was a Sweet thing to do to Cartor away off there, are now in order.
articles.summary: Quip on the marriage of Chicago pension agent Ada Sweet to a man named Carter.

articles.text: New York, for its size, is the stingiest city on the face of the globe. Bartholdi presented his immense statue to her and they have not succeeded in raising money to buy a pedestal. Not long ago they were going to build a $1,000,000 monument to Gen. Grant. They have succeeded, mostly through outside subscriptions, in raising the beggarly sum of $10,000 and there the project is likely to end. Chicago was scarcely a week in raising $50,000 for a monument fund.
articles.summary: Packard calls New York stingy over the Bartholdi statue pedestal and the Grant monument fund.

articles.text: The Black Hills Times is the only southern Dakota paper that dares tell the exact truth in reference to the true animus that actuates the prime movers in the statehood movement for South Dakota. Try to smooth over the matter as they will, the papers of southern Dakota must admit that the prominent leaders in their statehood movement and their present candidates for offices in their hoped-for state are in almost every case, chronic office-seekers and professional politicians. It is refreshing to see the Times nail the banner of truth to its mast-head and tell the truth about the whole matter. Show us a prominent mover in this statehood movement and we will show you a man who is preparing to warm his heels in some snug political berth. Show us a professional politician and we will instruct the house-wives of his neighborhood that it is unsafe for them to leave their washing out at night. To one who has seen anything of the all-absorbing selfishness and total lack of principle evinced by the average Dakota politician, the high-minded and patriotic stand those of the south take in attempting to form their new state, is so gauzy as to be ludicrous. The sole reason in their minds for wanting to make two states of Dakota, is to double the number of offices and consequently giving each politician twice as great a chance of securing one. Dakota admitted as a whole, will at once take a prominent position in the sisterhood of states. As two states, we would always be at the Rhode Island end. The recent election in the southern half of Dakota brought out only a fractional vote, showing the lack of interest there in the statehood movement and we fully believe that the whole vote would show a majority against division even in southern Dakota. The full vote of the Territory would show an enormous majority against division.
articles.summary: Packard praises the Black Hills Times and attacks the South Dakota statehood movement, arguing Dakota should be admitted whole and that a full vote would show a large majority against division.

articles.headline: Branding Cattle.
articles.text: The range business, it would seem, has another sin to answer for and it is one which affects everybody. It appears that by improper branding, thousands of hides are so injured that they are comparatively worthless. It is estimated that the loss from this source alone at Chicago is $2,000,000 a year and that throughout the entire country it will reach $5,000,000. But considerable leather that is damaged in this way gets into the leather articles that we use and of course is not so serviceable.. The cattlemen say that they cannot remedy the evil. They must brand and practically as they do now to protect their property. They cannot, they say, use smaller brands, for they could not be distinguished in rounding up. They cannot brand on a less valuable part of the hide, for the brand would not be prominent enough. That may all be true, but it does not help the tanners or the purchaser of an imperfect leather article. Five million dollars, too, is a pretty high cost for a method and to save that, ought to be sufficient motive to attempt to devise some less objectionable means to reach the desired end. But there is one fact that is plain enough to anyone who will examine these branded hides. Many of them are not properly done. They show that they have been done either by somebody who did not care how he did it or by somebody who was mad when he did it. The depth of the brand is often powerfully suggestive that the brute who did the work, became angry with the animal for some reason, and branded for punishment. In one conclusion all will agree and that is that there is no necessity of burning the animal clear through. A little sense and humane feeling would do much [to?] modify the evil complained of.
articles.summary: Article (identified by Packard as from the Western Rural) blaming improper, over-deep branding for millions of dollars in damaged hides.

articles.text: The above article, from the Western Rural, is in the main written in a fair spirit, but throughout, it shows the inaability common to all eastern writers, of putting themselves in the place of the cattlemen and looking at the matter from a range stand-point. The simple facts are as follows: A man's brand is his signification of ownership. According to range law, it is impossible for a man to claim an animal unless his brand is on it. As a natural consequence a man wants his brand to be as plain as possible. Another reason for wanting the brand plain, is that probably millions of dollars are saved yearly in word being sent concerning strays, as a ready means of identification when stolen, as a virtual insurance against theft if the brand is large and distinct, and in many other ways. The whole matter resolves itself to this: An unbranded animal can be claimed by no one, while the chances are that even should a well-branded animal stray a thousand miles from the home ranch, the owner will be as safe in finally getting full value for it as if he had kept it constantly in his barn. The Rural must remember that the range cattleman does not by any means see his cattle every day or every week or even every year. A plain brand, however, makes his ownership as secure as if they were constantly in sight. The Rural must also remember that tanners cut but a small figure in range profits; immeasurably less than the loss would be if animals were not branded. Then also, the question arises, will animals branded with a small brand or none at all, bring a higher price in the Chicago yards than those well branded? We have the answer from a man who is not only a practical tanner, owning one of the largest tanneries in New York state, but is also a large owner of range cattle, that the beef-producing qualities of an animal are alone taken into consideration by the buyer and proves his belief by branding with two large brands that about cover the side of the animal. Again, the cowmen are no more responsible for tanners using these damaged hides than they are for the grocer putting chicory in his coffee. He sells the carcass and the hide goes with it. Finally, let the Rural find some better plan than branding as a means of identification and we will guarantee that there will be a perfectly unanimous and willing change to it. No one appreciates the bad qualities of the present branding system more than the stockmen themselves.
articles.summary: Packard rebuts the Western Rural from the range standpoint: a large plain brand is the cattleman's proof of ownership and protection against loss and theft.

articles.headline: Aberdeen-Angus and Galloways.
articles.text: Black polled cattle have been bred in Scotland for hundreds of years, but no effort was made to improve them before 1700. Since that time, they have gradually grown in popular favor. At the Paris exposition in 1878, they were awarded first premium for best cattle of any breed and also championship prize for best group of beef-producing breeds. The first polled Scot introduced into this country was imported in 1872 and the demand for them is now so great that their yearly importations exceed that of any other breed. Most of these importations have been distributed among the western states, Missouri at present, having the largest number. Black polled cattle are divided into two classes, Aberdeen Angus, bred in northern Scotland and Galloways in southern. There are no very distinct points of difference in the two breeds. They are a hardy, fine boned, early-maturing race of cattle. Their hornless condition has contributed much to make them popular, for it is a [noticeable?] fact that stockmen are com[ing?] to consider horns as useless appendages and [illegible] shipping and stabling cattle. As a beef-producing breed, they are unsurpassed. In London, England, they command two cents a pound more than other beef. As a dairy breed, they excel many of the prominent horned breeds. They give a fair yield of very rich milk.—[Rural and Stockman.
articles.summary: Clipped piece (Rural and Stockman) on the history and merits of black polled Aberdeen-Angus and Galloway cattle.

articles.headline: Concerning the Range Cattle Industry.
articles.text:
In some portions of the range country a mistaken notion has prevailed in regard to [illegible]ing cheap southern cattle. It was argued by some that if the price of young cattle in the south was depressed the margin to the drover or the purchaser from the north, who went south to buy would be increased to the amount of the depression in the south. Results have proven this a fallacy. The blockading of the drives the past season and the quarantine against Texas cattle from below the thirty-fourth parallel caused a shrinkage of over $5 per head on all classes of Texas cattle, but in sympathy with this decline values have gone off equally as much all along the line from Texas to Montana. And this will always be the rule. There is a sympathetic connection between values of any article of traffic which is as certain and true as the magnetic needle. Commerce is argus-eyed, and at once discovers the means for restoring any temporarily disturbed equilibrium in trade or values.

A very large per cent. of the cattle on the northern ranges have been graded up from Texas cows. In 1881 there was a large drive from Oregon and Washington territory, and since that time a good many young cattle and some cows have been shipped in from Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri and a few other states. These "pilgrim" cattle from the east have not shown as ready adaptation to range life as the western and Texas imports, and the tendency is rather to discourage the traffic in them. Raised on the pitchfork, so to speak, they know nothing of self-dependence, and when the winter storm strikes them they naturally look for man's help, and fail to "rustle" for themselves. On the contrary, the western and southern cattle for generations have had to make their own provision for winter, and are always found rustling for something to eat. But the southern cattle are of light weight, and as increased weight means increased profits, northern ranchmen have for years been buying high grade bulls from the east and grading up their herds. The native cattle today on all the northern ranges are as good or perhaps a little better than half-breeds. Shorthorns and Herefords are, as a rule, the improved breeds used, and our three and four-year-old steers weigh from 1,100 to 1,300 pounds in the Chicago market.

This makes a very profitable animal when the markets are not broken by too large receipts, and the question is being generally discussed among ranchmen as to whether the herds are not sufficiently graded up to be safe and profitable. A few herd owners claim that a thoroughbred animal will sustain as much hardship and do as much rustling for food as the scrub or grade, but the general opinion is that the rustling qualities belong to the scrub, and that grading up means a larger carcass at the expense of the ability to endure the necessary hardships of our northern winters. The practical point to determine is, how high can we grade without losing the self sustaining qualities? Large, well-shaped and weighty cattle are desirable, but if the mortality is increased beyond the gain in size, the improvement is a mistake. Sufficient experiment has not yet been made to definitely determine this point. Present information leads to the opinion that in time there will be established a fixed type of range cattle: something better than a half-breed Shorthorn or Hereford, but developed by a blending of beef breeds. The Swiss cattle have been produced in this way, and they are a very good "all purpose" animal. No particular strain of blood can be traced in them, yet they are uniform in characteristics. With a range animal built up after a good model, uniform in size, containing all the improved blood consistent with a retention of the "rustling" qualities would tend to create a more uniform market. At present the periodical breaks in the beef market are caused by the sending in of unripe animals, or those that are ill-shaped in undue proportion. Uniformity in size and appearance will do much to maintain evenness in market values. There is room for marked improvement in many ways touching range management, but perhaps the most important is the one above named, for securing the best animal, and then ascertaining how to hold on to the proper type.—[Texas Stockman.
articles.summary: Clipped essay (Texas Stockman) on Texas cattle values, "pilgrim" cattle from the east, and how far northern range herds should be graded up.

articles.text: Some years ago the world was treated to stories, which tested the credulity of readers, respecting the Brobdignagian farms of great land proprietors in the far west. Farms proportioned rather to the more liberal dimensions of Saturn or Jupiter than to the cramped bounds of this tiny planet were reported, where the eye was wearied with gazing on crops by the square mile, cultivated by steam plows driven in platoons. All this was magnificent, but it was not farming. At least, according to Theodore Roosevelt, who had been studying up that subject, the big farms do not pay. He says that in nearly every case where the experiment has been tried the result has been the collapse of the wealthy capitalist or corporation. The one big farm, he finds, cannot compete with the many small ones, side by side with, it each of which is carefully and economically tilled by its frugal owner. And it is fortunate that such has proved to be the case, for the prosperity of a new settlement depends on the success of small farms managed in person by their owners.
articles.summary: Syndicated paragraph on the patent page citing Theodore Roosevelt's view that big bonanza farms do not pay; transcribed only because it names Roosevelt.

articles.text: Go to the Drug Store for jewelry, silver plated ware, etc.
articles.summary: Drug Store offers jewelry and silver plated ware.

articles.text: If you are in need of a good tea-set either in figured gold or china, H. M. Jorgens can fit you out.
articles.summary: H. M. Jorgens sells tea-sets.

articles.text: H. M. Jorgens has just opened up a complete stock of crockery and glassware. Now is your time to purchase.
articles.summary: Jorgens opens a stock of crockery and glassware.

articles.text: The Marquis started for New York Tuesday morning, to be gone until the latter part of February. He expects to visit France before his return.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès left for New York Tuesday, to be away until late February and expecting to visit France.

articles.text: The sale of Jack Bullion's ponies took place Monday forenoon. Sixteen were sold altogether, averaging about twenty dollars each. The price was lower than expected.
articles.summary: Sixteen of Jack Bullion's ponies sold Monday at about $20 each.

articles.text: Congrtulations are in order and for the last week have been showered on James Butler and wife. Their Thanksgiving present was in the shape of a thirteen-and-a-half pound baby boy. Mother and son are doing finely.
articles.summary: James Butler and wife had a 13½-pound baby boy at Thanksgiving.

articles.text: Christmas is coming and you can get anything you want in the way of presents of H. M. Jorgens.
articles.summary: Jorgens advertises Christmas presents.

articles.text: From all quarters come favorable reports as to the condition of stock. The cattle in the Bad Lands are all in good condition at present and for the most part, will winter well. Prairie fires and the over-crowding of ranges will in some cases make a scant supply of feed, but the cattle will drift enough to regulate this.
articles.summary: Bad Lands cattle reported in good condition for winter, though fires and overcrowding have thinned feed in places.

articles.text: H. M. Jorgens wishes to announce to the public that he has connected with his business a gift enterprise. Buying three dollars' worth of fancy goods, notions or jewelry entitles you to a number in the gift enterprise. Every number draws a prize varying in price from ten cents to ten dollars.
articles.summary: Jorgens starts a gift enterprise: each $3 purchase earns a numbered prize draw.

articles.text: The case of Geo. Fitzgerald against Gregor Lang was settled yesterday by the latter buying the former's brand. This was altogether better than going to law on the subject, as the matter throughout was a mistake, there being no suspicion of criminal intent.
articles.summary: Fitzgerald's case against Gregor Lang settled Wednesday when Lang bought Fitzgerald's brand.

articles.text: The Drug store is the place to buy anything you want in the way of fancy goods or notions.
articles.summary: Drug store fancy goods.

articles.text: The hunting party we spoke of last week, consistsng of Messers Fisher, Paddock and McGregor, came back laden with thirteen deer and eighty-five prairie chickens.
articles.summary: Fisher, Paddock and McGregor return from a hunt with 13 deer and 85 prairie chickens.

articles.text: Dr. Jorgens has received some fresh vaccine virus and everyone should make a point of being vaccinated immediately. A simple operation now may save your life.
articles.summary: Dr. Jorgens has fresh vaccine and urges vaccination.

articles.text: Miss Jennie Macbeth left for her home in Mankato, Minn., yesterday morning. She is followed by the regards of a wide circle of friends and wishes for her return are numerous.
articles.summary: Miss Jennie Macbeth left Wednesday for her home in Mankato, Minn.

articles.text: Remember that you can buy your fancy goods and notions as cheap at the Drug store in Medora as you can anywhere this side of St. Paul. Besides this you may draw a prize to exceed the value of the goods.
articles.summary: Drug store prices and prize drawing.

articles.text: Although it is rather doubtful, there may be some one whose name has not been mentioned for an office. If so let him see to it that the ommission be corrected. We may as well be unanimous about the thing.
articles.summary: Packard jokes that nearly everyone has been mentioned for a county office.

articles.text: Politics are the all-absorbing topic apparently and we have heard a number of tickets proposed. We are still in favor of the one we published in the Cow Boy some time ago.
articles.summary: Several county tickets are being proposed; the Cow Boy still favors the one it published earlier.

articles.text: A letter from the Govenor seems to indicate that our county will be organized about the middle of January. He promises to take immediate steps in the matter and a call for an election will soon be issued.
articles.summary: A letter from the Governor indicates Billings county will be organized about mid-January, with an election call soon.

articles.text: The dance given Thanksgiving evening at the Maltese cross ranch is still a topic of conversation. Everyone who went had a splendid time and Merrifield & Ferris added fresh honor to themselves as accomplished hosts.
articles.summary: Thanksgiving-evening dance at the Maltese Cross ranch, hosted by Merrifield & Ferris.

articles.text: School began last Monday morning in Medora hall, with Edward Simmers as teacher. Twenty-two scholars are in attendance and others will soon join. Every thing will soon be in good running shape, unless we are mistaken in Mr. Simmers' capabilities. We suggest that parents and friends make a practice of visiting the school occasionally. It is a wonderful incentive to both teacher and scholars.
articles.summary: School opened Monday in Medora hall under teacher Edward Simmers, with 22 scholars.
